questions.problem: Let $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-2x+y \\ -x+4y \\ -3x-5y\end{aligned}]$ be a linear transformation. Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4 \\ k\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]$ such that $T(u)=v.$ 

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2x+y \\ -x+4y \\ -3x-5y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2x+y=6 \\ -x+4y=-4 \\ -3x-5y=k.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=4+4y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+y & =6 \\ -2(4+4y)+y & =6 \\ -7y & =14 \\ y & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4+4y \\  & =4+4(-2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-4$ and $y=-2$ into the third equation and obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x-5y & =k \\ -3(-4)-5(-2) & =k \\ k & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=22.$

questions.problem: Let $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+y \\ x+2y \\ -2x+7y\end{aligned}]$ be a linear transformation. Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 8 \\ k\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]$ such that $T(u)=v.$ 

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3x+y \\ x+2y \\ -2x+7y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 8 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x+y=9 \\ x+2y=8 \\ -2x+7y=k.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=8-2y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+y & =9 \\ 3(8-2y)+y & =9 \\ -5y & =-15 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =8-2y \\  & =8-2(3) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=2$ and $y=3$ into the third equation and obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+7y & =k \\ -2(2)+7(3) & =k \\ k & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=17.$

questions.problem: Let $T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]$ be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{aligned}]$  belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]$ such that $T(u)=v.$

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot u & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2x-4y \\ x-3y \\ -x+4y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 7 \\ k\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x-4y=2 \\ x-3y=7 \\ -x+4y=k.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x=7+3y$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4y & =2 \\ 2(7+3y)-4y & =2 \\ 2y & =-12 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7+3y \\  & =7+3(-6) \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=-11$ and $y=-6$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+4y & =k \\ -(-11)+4(-6) & =k \\ k & =-13.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=-13.$

questions.problem: Let $T=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -5 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]$ be the standard matrix of the linear transformation $T.$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ k \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
The vector $v$ belongs to $\text{Im}(T)$ if there exists a vector $u=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]$ such that $T(u)=v.$

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot u & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ -5 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ k \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3x+2y \\ -2y \\ -5x+y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ k \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3x+2y=5 \\ -2y=k \\ -5x+y=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $y=5x-1$, which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+2y & =5 \\ -3x+2(5x-1) & =5 \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5x-1 \\  & =5(1)-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=4$ into the second equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2y & =k \\ -2(4) & =k \\ k & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $v\in \text{Im}(T)$ when $k=-8.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Vector Is in the Image of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 \\ -2 & -4 & 4\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -28 \\ 26\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -5 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 & -28 \\ -2 & -4 & 4 & 26\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & -4 & 8 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=-8\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-4+2{x}_{3}.
$$

From the first equation we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+2{x}_{3}=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-5-2{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-5-2{x}_{3} \\ -4+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=1$, we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-7+(-2)=-9.$

questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{4}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of $w-x+y,$ where $w,x,y,z$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}w \\ x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}w-3x-2z \\ 2x-2w-4y \\ 3w-y-10x-7z \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & -10 & -1 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 2 & -4 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & -10 & -1 & -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 & -1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get the false statement $0=-8.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$

questions.problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -7 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 4 & -1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -11 & 11 & 11 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{11}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -11 & 11 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
-11{x}_{2}+11{x}_{3}=11\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-1+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
-2{x}_{1}-5(-1+{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=9\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2-{x}_{3} \\ -1+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2-1=-3.$

In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}-{x}_{3},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}-{x}_{4} \\ -{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}+{x}_{4} \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4} \\ -11{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -5 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-1){R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -2 & 11 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get the false statement $0=-6.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$

questions.problem: Given the transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+y+z \\ z+y-x \\ z-2y\end{aligned}],$ find its rank.
questions.worked_solution:
First, the standard matrix of $T$ is given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Im}(T))=\text{rank}(T).$ 

So, we need to find the rank of the matrix $T.$ We reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $T$ has $3$ pivot columns, we have that 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Im}(T))=\text{rank}(T).$ 

So, we need to find the rank of the matrix $T.$ We reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 14 & -14 \\ 2 & 3 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 14 & -14 \\ 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{14}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 14 & -14 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $T$ has $2$ pivot columns, we have that 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=2.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/1c8969401a7c812e945fdc0b2f1774f6cd1d1d9c35269b2b20ea8165449d427f.png) be a linear transformation. Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/05f7384dd957b2616433104bfefbb8b3e7aaa619dbb1dff94fec43c8a99e6c3c.png) belongs to $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The vector $\mathbf{v}$ belongs to $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})$ if there exists a vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/be82bf02cdfe6a50557b312ba78708463248f844f81016df2cda41c6cfbb6c1a.png) such that $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{v}.$ 

Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ -x+y \\ 2y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ k \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y=4 \\ -x+y=k \\ 2y=8.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $y=4,$ which we substitute into the first equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+4 & =4 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $x=0$ and $y=4$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+y & =k \\ 0+4 & =k \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf{v}\in\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})$ when $k=4.$

canonical_examples.problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ and the vector $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{b}.$ In the affirmative case, find such a vector.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/36675dd67326016b3083bfb87ec93ae427a74879ce41007a4cadf11f6cfca80d.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $\mathbf{T},$ we have $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}) = \textrm{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $\mathbf{b}$ lies in $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T}),$ we need to check if the equation $T\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T \,|\, \mathbf{b}],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 2 & 6 \\ 6 & 4 & -10 & 26 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & -8 & -16 & 8 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & -8 & -16 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has a zero row, and so the system is consistent. We have two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). So, $x_3$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
-8x_2-16x_3 = 8
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_2=-1-2x_3.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
2x_1+4(-1-2x_3)+2x_3 = 6
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=5+3x_3.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/72aba565539bdf6cee541e7495665a5bd422f8e7c5693ab68794c0a284c42e8d.png)

Setting $x_3=0,$ we have

canonical_examples.problem: If ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071327/assets/71adf512017629aa4cfc010c18bc840ea63459818bae4ebc0b7dba59193c0d00.png) is the standard matrix of the linear transformation $\mathbf{T},$ then what is $\text{rank}(\mathbf{T})?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In general, $\text{rank}(\mathbf{T}) = \text{dim}(\text{Im}(\mathbf{T})) = \text{rank}(T).$ 

So, we need to find the rank of the matrix $T.$ We reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 & -2 \\ -6 & 5 & -1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 7 & 7 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{7}{4}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $T$ has $2$ pivot columns, we have that 

$$
\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{rank}(T)=2.
$$
